nameStory: The Antelope Beetle gets its striking name from the male's impressive mandibles (jaws) that branch and curve like the horns of an antelope. These "antler-like" projections aren't just for show — males use them like wrestlers' arms to grapple with rivals during mating season. It's sometimes called the Weaver Beetle, though the origin of that alternate name remains a bit of a mystery to beetle enthusiasts.
description: The Antelope Beetle is one of New England's most impressive stag beetles, belonging to a family known for their enlarged mandibles that look like tiny deer antlers. Males are the real showstoppers, sporting dramatic curved jaws that can be nearly as long as their bodies. These robust, dark-colored beetles are among the larger species you'll encounter in our region. Like all stag beetles, they have that classic hard-shelled, armor-plated appearance that makes them look like tiny knights of the insect world.

idTips.label: Male mandibles
idTips.description: Large, curved, antler-like jaws that branch and feel hard as plastic when touched (handle gently). These impressive mandibles are the beetle's signature feature.

idTips.label: Body size
idTips.description: Notably large and robust with a heavy, solid feel when picked up. The body has a substantial weight that distinguishes it from smaller beetle species.

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Deep brown to black shiny exterior that feels smooth and hard like polished wood. The surface reflects light with a glossy sheen.

idTips.label: Female appearance
idTips.description: Females lack the dramatic mandibles but share the same robust build and dark coloring. Their jaws are much smaller and more proportional to their head.

idTips.label: Wing covers
idTips.description: Hard wing covers (elytra) that feel like thick plastic and often show fine ridges or lines when examined closely.

habitat: Look for Antelope Beetles in deciduous and mixed forests where they're associated with decaying hardwood, particularly oak and maple. They prefer areas with rich, moist soil and plenty of fallen logs or dead wood where larvae can develop. You might spot adults around outdoor lights at night or crawling on tree trunks in wooded areas throughout New England's lower elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their underground pupation sites. Look for them starting to appear around decaying logs and tree bases as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and active. Males can be found wrestling over territory and mates, while both sexes may be attracted to outdoor lights at night.
seasonality.fall: Adults are still active but beginning to slow down. This is when mated females are busy laying eggs in decaying wood where larvae will spend the next year or more developing.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and larvae are developing underground in rotting wood. No surface activity to observe during the cold months.

funFact: Despite their fearsome-looking mandibles, male Antelope Beetles are essentially gentle giants — their impressive jaws are too specialized for wrestling other males to deliver a painful bite to humans, making them safe to handle with basic care.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other stag beetles, but the Antelope Beetle's distinctly branched, antler-like mandibles set it apart from species with simpler jaw shapes. Remember: if the male's jaws look like they belong on a tiny deer, you've found your antelope!
contextualKnowledge: This species is part of a fascinating family where males often look dramatically different from females due to their enlarged mandibles. The scientific name "parallelus" refers to the parallel-sided shape of the body, which is more apparent in preserved specimens than living beetles.
compareHints: As the only Dorcus species regularly found in New England, the Antelope Beetle stands apart from other regional stag beetles by its particular mandible shape and robust build. While other stag beetles in our area may have enlarged male jaws, none have the distinctive branched, antler-like appearance that gives this species its memorable common name.
